docs.title: vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position
docs.text:
Vertical (Z) coordinate of the electron cyclotron wave launching position, specifying the height of the launcher above or below the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

The vertical coordinate \(Z_{\rm launch}\) locates the point at which an electron cyclotron (EC) beam enters the plasma in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, where \(Z\) measures height relative to the machine midplane, \(R\) is the major radius from the symmetry axis, and \(\phi\) is the toroidal angle. Together with major_radius_of_launching_position, it fully specifies the poloidal-plane position of the EC launcher aperture, which determines the initial ray trajectory used in beam-tracing or ray-tracing codes to model wave propagation and absorption in the plasma. Typical values range from approximately \(-2\) m to \(+2\) m for medium-to-large tokamaks, depending on launcher installation height and whether the beam is aimed from the low-field or high-field side. The launching position is usually defined at the antenna mirror or waveguide mouth and is provided as a fixed geometric parameter in the launcher design documentation or inferred from engineering surveys; it pairs with the mirror orientation angles described by toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror to fully characterize the beam injection geometry.

Sign convention: Positive when the launching position lies above the machine midplane in the \(+Z\) direction.

docs.title: vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position
docs.text:
Vertical Z coordinate locating a generic diagnostic or reflectometer measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, where \(Z\) is the height above or below the machine midplane.

The vertical coordinate \(Z\) specifies the height of a measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis, \(\phi\) is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and \(Z\) is the vertical height in meters. This generic locus token applies across multiple diagnostic systems — including reflectometers, interferometers, ECE radiometers, flux loops, and barometry gages — where the measurement position is defined by a single spatial point rather than an endpoint of a line of sight. Typical values range from approximately \(-2\) m to \(+2\) m for medium-to-large tokamaks, with \(Z = 0\) at the machine midplane. For more precisely defined geometric loci on diagnostic lines of sight, see vertical_coordinate_of_first_point_of_line_of_sight, vertical_coordinate_of_second_point_of_line_of_sight, and vertical_coordinate_of_third_point_of_line_of_sight; for antenna-based diagnostics see vertical_coordinate_of_centroid_of_diagnostic_antenna. The companion major-radius coordinate for the same measurement position is major_radius_of_launching_position for launcher-type diagnostics.

Sign convention: Positive when the measurement position is above the machine midplane in the \(+Z\) direction of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

docs.title: x_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
X-axis projection of the unit vector that encodes the instantaneous movement direction of the steerable electron cyclotron (EC) launcher mirror in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

The EC launcher mirror movement direction is fully specified by the unit vector \(\hat{d} = (d_x, d_y, d_z)\), where \(d_x\) is this quantity. Because \(\hat{d}\) is a unit vector by construction, the three Cartesian components satisfy \(d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1\), so \(d_x \in [-1, 1]\). The mirror direction vector describes how the reflective surface tilts or rotates to steer the injected high-power microwave beam toward the desired deposition location inside the plasma; the \(\hat{x}\) component captures the projection of that motion onto the machine Cartesian \(x\)-axis. In practice, \(d_x\) is either set by a geometric model of the launcher mechanism or read directly from mirror position encoders, and it enters beam-tracing and ray-tracing codes that compute the electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) or electron cyclotron current drive (ECCD) power deposition profile. Together with the companion components y_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and z_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, it reconstructs the full direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror. The orientation frame of the mirror itself is separately described by the local unit-vector triad, whose x-projections include x_component_of_first_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror.

Sign convention: Positive when the mirror movement direction has a component in the \(+\hat{x}\) direction of the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

Unit: 1

Kind: scalar

docs.title: y_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
Y-axis projection of the unit vector encoding the instantaneous movement direction of the steerable electron cyclotron (EC) launcher mirror in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

The quantity \(d_y = \hat{d} \cdot \hat{y}\) is the \(y\)-component of the mirror direction unit vector \(\hat{d} = (d_x, d_y, d_z)\), which specifies how the EC launcher mirror is currently moving as it steers the injected microwave beam toward its intended deposition location in the plasma. Together with x_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and z_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, it completes the Cartesian triplet satisfying the unit-vector constraint \(d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1\). The parent quantity direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror encodes the full three-dimensional movement direction; this component isolates the horizontal \(y\)-axis contribution in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame co-located with the launcher assembly. The component is dimensionless and bounded on \([-1, 1]\); a value of \(\pm 1\) indicates movement purely along \(\pm\hat{y}\), while zero means the mirror moves with no \(y\)-axis component. This quantity is used in beam-steering control systems and ray-tracing codes to compute the beam injection angle and the corresponding deposition location in the plasma, complementing the orientation frame defined by first_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and second_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror.

Sign convention: Positive when the mirror movement direction has a component along \(+\hat{y}\) in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

docs.title: z_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
Vertical component of the unit direction vector that encodes the instantaneous movement direction of the steerable EC launcher mirror in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame, where \(\hat{z}\) is aligned with the machine vertical axis \(Z\).

The Z-component \(d_z\) of the direction unit vector of the EC launcher mirror specifies how much of the mirror's instantaneous movement direction projects onto the vertical axis \(\hat{z}\) of the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame, where \(\hat{z}\) coincides with the machine vertical direction. Because the parent vector is a unit vector by construction, the three Cartesian components satisfy \(d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1\), so \(d_z \in [-1, 1]\). A value of \(d_z = \pm 1\) indicates purely vertical mirror movement, while \(d_z = 0\) means the movement lies entirely in the horizontal plane. This component, together with x_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and y_component_of_direction_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, fully resolves the mirror movement direction needed for beam-steering calculations in electron cyclotron heating and current drive systems. The direction vector is typically obtained from launcher geometry specifications or actuator kinematics models and is used in ray-tracing and beam-tracing codes to propagate the injected microwave beam trajectory through the plasma.

Sign convention: Positive when the mirror movement direction has a component in the \(+\hat{z}\) direction (upward, toward increasing \(Z\)).

docs.title: height_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap
docs.text:
Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor, defining its extent in the poloidal (Z) direction.

The height of an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna strap is the full vertical extent of its rectangular cross-section, measured along the \(Z\) axis of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame where \(Z\) is the vertical coordinate. Together with width and thickness, this dimension fully characterizes the cross-sectional geometry of the strap conductor, which governs its current-carrying capacity, RF impedance, and thermal loading during high-power operation. The strap cross-sectional geometry is a fixed engineering parameter specified at design time and verified by metrology; typical heights for tokamak ICRH straps fall in the range of a few centimeters to tens of centimeters depending on the machine size and power requirements. The vertical coordinate of the rectangle center locates the strap in the poloidal plane, while the length describes the strap's extent along its principal conductor axis.

Sign convention: Positive when the height extends in the direction of increasing \(Z\) (upward from the machine midplane).

docs.title: length_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap
docs.text: Length of an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna strap conductor measured along its longest axis in the oblique cross-sectional geometry, corresponding to the strap's extent in the direction perpendicular to its cross-section plane. This dimension is distinct from the strap width and thickness, which characterize the cross-sectional face.

docs.title: Length of ICRH Antenna Strap
docs.text:
This quantity specifies the length of an individual strap conductor belonging to an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna module, as stored at ic_antennas/antenna/module/strap/geometry/oblique/length in the IMAS data dictionary.

In the oblique strap geometry, the strap is characterized by three independent linear dimensions: - length: the extent along the strap's longest (longitudinal) axis, i.e., the dimension perpendicular to the oblique cross-sectional face; - width: the cross-sectional dimension in the poloidal or toroidal direction, depending on strap orientation; - height (or thickness): the remaining cross-sectional dimension.

The length dimension governs the resonant electrical behavior of the strap and is a key parameter in antenna modeling codes (e.g., TOPICA, ANTITER). Typical ICRH strap lengths on medium-to-large tokamaks range from approximately \(0.3\,\mathrm{m}\) to \(1.5\,\mathrm{m}\), consistent with quarter-wave or half-wave resonance conditions at frequencies in the range \(25\text{–}120\,\mathrm{MHz}\).

The oblique geometry means the strap cross-section is not necessarily aligned with the cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame; the length is always measured along the conductor's own longitudinal axis regardless of its orientation in the machine. When precise directional decomposition is required, companion quantities such as the toroidal component of the strap width should be consulted.

docs.title: z_component_of_second_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
Projection of the second local unit vector of the electron cyclotron launcher mirror orientation frame onto the vertical axis \(\hat{z}\) of the right-handed Cartesian frame, where \(\hat{z}\) coincides with the machine vertical direction \(\hat{Z}\).

The Z component \(\hat{e}_{2,z}\) is the projection of the second axis of the orthonormal triad \(\{\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{e}_3\}\) onto the vertical direction \(\hat{z}\), which coincides with \(\hat{Z}\) in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame. Together with the Y component y_component_of_second_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, this component fully specifies the second unit vector in the plane perpendicular to \(\hat{x}\), completing the second_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror. Because \(\hat{e}_2\) is a unit vector, the identity \(\hat{e}_{2,x}^2 + \hat{e}_{2,y}^2 + \hat{e}_{2,z}^2 = 1\) must hold; values of this component are therefore constrained to \([-1, 1]\). In conjunction with z_component_of_first_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and z_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, this quantity defines the full third row of the rotation matrix that transforms between the mirror local frame and the laboratory Cartesian frame, directly determining the vertical component of the beam steering geometry for electron cyclotron heating calculations.

Sign convention: Positive when the second unit vector \(\hat{e}_2\) has a component pointing in the \(+\hat{z}\) (upward) direction of the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

docs.title: x_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
X-axis projection of the third unit vector in the orthonormal triad that defines the local orientation frame of an electron cyclotron (EC) launcher mirror, expressed in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

The third unit vector of the EC launcher mirror completes the right-handed orthonormal triad that fully specifies the mirror's spatial orientation for beam-steering calculations. Its \(x\)-component is the dot product \(\hat{e}_3 \cdot \hat{x}\), where \(\hat{e}_3\) is the third local axis of the mirror frame and \(\hat{x}\) is the global Cartesian axis in the right-handed \(( \hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame with \(\hat{z}\) vertical. Together with the y-component and the z-component, the three Cartesian projections satisfy \(e_{3x}^2 + e_{3y}^2 + e_{3z}^2 = 1\) by construction. The triad is determined from the mechanical geometry of the launcher, with the third axis often aligned with the mirror normal or a defined reference direction; values therefore lie in \([-1, 1]\) and are set at configuration time rather than measured dynamically. The x-component of the first unit vector and the x-component of the direction unit vector are the analogous projections for the first axis and the mirror movement direction, respectively.

Sign convention: Positive when the third unit vector has a positive projection onto the \(+\hat{x}\) Cartesian axis.

docs.title: z_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror
docs.text:
Vertical component of the third local unit vector that completes the right-handed orthonormal orientation frame of an electron cyclotron (EC) launcher mirror, projected onto the \(\hat{z}\) axis of the Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

The EC launcher mirror orientation is fully specified by three mutually orthogonal unit vectors. This quantity gives the \(\hat{z}\) projection of the third vector, \(\hat{e}_3\), of that triad: \(z_3 = \hat{e}_3 \cdot \hat{z}\), where \(\hat{z}\) is the vertical axis of the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame. Because \(\hat{e}_3\) is a unit vector, this component is bounded in \([-1, 1]\), and together with x_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and y_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror it satisfies \(x_3^2 + y_3^2 + z_3^2 = 1\). The third unit vector completes the triad formed with first_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror and second_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror, fully encoding the mirror pointing geometry needed for beam-steering calculations; see the parent vector third_unit_vector_of_electron_cyclotron_launcher_mirror for the full vector definition. The \(z\)-component is particularly sensitive to the mirror tilt relative to the horizontal plane and is zero when \(\hat{e}_3\) lies entirely in the \(xy\)-plane. Values are derived from the mirror mechanical geometry or from in-situ survey measurements of the launcher orientation.

Sign convention: Positive when the third unit vector has a component in the \(+\hat{z}\) (upward vertical) direction.

docs.title: x_component_of_third_unit_vector_of_beam_source
docs.text:
X-axis projection of the third local unit vector that completes the right-handed orientation frame of a beam source, diagnostic aperture, or optical element in the Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

The third unit vector \(\hat{e}_3\) of a beam source forms the third axis of a right-handed local orthonormal triad \(\{\hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \hat{e}_3\}\) that fully specifies the geometric orientation of the source or aperture element. Its x-component is the projection \(e_{3,x} = \hat{e}_3 \cdot \hat{x}\), where \(\hat{x}\) is the Cartesian axis in the right-handed frame \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) with \(\hat{z}\) vertical. Because \(\hat{e}_3\) is a unit vector, its three Cartesian projections satisfy \(e_{3,x}^2 + e_{3,y}^2 + e_{3,z}^2 = 1\), so this component is bounded in \([-1, 1]\). In practice the triad is determined from engineering survey data or from the geometric configuration of the NBI injector, EC mirror, or diagnostic filter window, and is used to transform beam-aligned quantities into the machine Cartesian frame for ray-tracing and power-deposition calculations. The complementary projections are captured by the y- and z-components of the same vector, and the full orientation context is provided by third_unit_vector_of_beam_source. The first and second unit vectors of the same frame are described by the analogous families whose x-components are x_component_of_first_unit_vector_of_beam_source; the same decomposition for diagnostic antennas is third_unit_vector_x_component_of_diagnostic_antenna.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of \(\hat{e}_3\) onto \(\hat{x}\) is in the direction of increasing \(x\) in the right-handed Cartesian \((\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})\) frame.

docs.title: toroidal_component_of_width_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap
docs.text:
Toroidal extent of an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna strap, measuring the arc length or linear dimension of the strap conductor along the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\).

The toroidal width of an ICRH antenna strap defines the dimension of the strap conductor measured along the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. This dimension directly governs the toroidal current distribution on the strap and influences the antenna's coupling resistance and the spectrum of waves launched into the plasma; a wider strap shifts the parallel wave-number spectrum \(k_\parallel\) toward lower values. Together with width_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap (the horizontal cross-sectional width), height_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap (the poloidal extent), and thickness_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna_strap (the depth), this quantity fully characterizes the strap conductor geometry for electromagnetic modeling of antenna-plasma coupling. Typical values range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters depending on the machine size and antenna design, with ITER-scale straps spanning on the order of 0.1–0.3 m in the toroidal direction. The value is determined from engineering drawings or direct metrology of the fabricated antenna structure.

Sign convention: Positive when the strap extent is measured in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\).

docs.title: poloidal_component_of_anomalous_current_density
docs.text:
Poloidal projection of the anomalous (non-classical) current density in the edge plasma. Defined as the dot product of the anomalous current density vector with the local poloidal unit vector. Contributions arise from turbulence-driven transport processes not captured by classical or neoclassical theory.

The poloidal component of the anomalous current density is defined as

\[j_{\mathrm{ano},\theta} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{ano}} \cdot \hat{e}_{\theta}\]

where \(\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{ano}}\) is the anomalous (non-classical) current density vector and \(\hat{e}_{\theta}\) is the local poloidal unit vector directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle \(\theta\) in the flux surface geometry \((\psi, \theta, \phi)\).

The poloidal component is particularly relevant for characterizing bootstrap-like and turbulence-driven current structures in the edge region.

docs.title: radial_component_of_anomalous_current_density
docs.text:
Radial projection of the anomalous (non-classical) current density, quantifying cross-field current driven by turbulent or transport processes that are not captured by classical collisional theory in the edge and scrape-off-layer plasma.

Anomalous current density arises from plasma transport mechanisms beyond classical collisional theory — principally turbulence-driven fluctuations, anomalous diffusion, and non-classical drift terms in the edge plasma. The radial component \(j_{r,\mathrm{anom}}\) projects the full anomalous_current_density vector onto the flux-surface-normal (radial) direction, capturing cross-field charge transport that does not average to zero over a flux surface. In the edge and scrape-off layer, this component is relevant to radial electric field generation, \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\) flow drive, and the radial current balance $ abla \cdot \mathbf{j} = 0$. It is typically evaluated from fluid or gyrokinetic edge codes and is distinct from the neoclassical radial_component_of_pfirsch_schlueter_current_density, which arises from toroidal geometry effects alone. In turbulent edge plasmas, typical magnitudes range from \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{2}\) A m\(^{-2}\) depending on the turbulence level and plasma regime. The complementary components of the same vector are poloidal_component_of_anomalous_current_density, toroidal_component_of_anomalous_current_density, and parallel_component_of_anomalous_current_density.

Sign convention: Positive when the anomalous current density component points in the direction of increasing major radius \(R\) (outward radial direction in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame).

docs.title: toroidal_component_of_anomalous_current_density
docs.text:
Projection of the anomalous (non-classical) current density onto the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\), isolating the \(\phi\)-directed component of turbulence-driven current not captured by classical or neoclassical transport theory.

The toroidal component \(J_{\mathrm{anom},\phi} = \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{anom}} \cdot \hat{\phi}\) quantifies the net charge flux in the toroidal direction arising from transport mechanisms — principally plasma turbulence, anomalous cross-field diffusion, and related non-classical processes — that lie outside collisional resistivity, bootstrap, or Pfirsch-Schlüter theory. Together with poloidal_component_of_anomalous_current_density, radial_component_of_anomalous_current_density, and parallel_component_of_anomalous_current_density, it completes the vector decomposition of anomalous_current_density in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. It is obtained from fluid or kinetic edge-plasma simulations (e.g., two-fluid or gyrofluid codes) by projecting the computed anomalous current vector onto \(\hat{\phi}\); direct experimental measurement requires subtraction of all classical and neoclassical contributions from the total toroidal current density.

docs.title: vertical_component_of_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
docs.text:
Projection of the ion-neutral friction current density onto the vertical \(\hat{Z}\) direction in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, quantifying the \(Z\)-component of charge current driven by collisional momentum exchange between ions and neutrals in the edge plasma.

In partially ionized edge and divertor plasmas, collisional friction between ions and neutral particles (via charge-exchange and elastic collisions) generates a current density vector \(\mathbf{j}_{\rm in}\). The vertical component extracts the \(Z\)-directed projection \(j_{\rm in,Z} = \mathbf{j}_{\rm in} \cdot \hat{Z}\), where \(\hat{Z}\) is the unit vector along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame with \(R\) the major radius and \(Z\) the vertical height. This component captures vertical charge transport driven by frictional momentum exchange and is physically relevant near X-points and divertor targets where strong vertical gradients and neutral recycling occur. It complements the toroidal component and parallel component of the same current, together with which it fully resolves the vector current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction. Related divergence-driven current contributions in the edge include the Pfirsch-Schlüter current density and the poloidal component of the current density due to parallel viscosity. Computed from multi-fluid or fluid-neutral edge transport codes on unstructured grids; magnitudes are typically in the range \(10^{3}\)–\(10^{6}\) A m\(^{-2}\) in divertor and recycling regions.

Sign convention: Positive when \(j_{\rm in,Z}\) points in the direction of increasing \(Z\) (upward along the machine symmetry axis).

docs.title: parallel_component_of_ion_state_momentum_flux
docs.text:
Parallel component of the momentum flux tensor for a specific ion charge state, obtained by projecting the full momentum flux onto the local magnetic field direction. This quantity captures the field-aligned transport of ion momentum per unit area for that charge state in the edge plasma.

The parallel component of the momentum flux tensor for a specific ion charge state is defined as the projection of the momentum flux density tensor \(\mathbf{\Pi}_s\) of ion charge state \(s\) onto the unit vector \(\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|\) along the local magnetic field:

\[\Pi_{\parallel,s} = \hat{b} \cdot \mathbf{\Pi}_s \cdot \hat{b} = \rho_s v_{\parallel,s}^2 + p_{\parallel,s}\]

where \(\rho_s\) (kg m\(^{-3}\)) is the mass density of charge state \(s\), \(v_{\parallel,s}\) (m s\(^{-1}\)) is the parallel fluid velocity of that charge state, and \(p_{\parallel,s}\) (Pa = kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\)) is the parallel component of the (potentially anisotropic) pressure tensor for that charge state. In a magnetized edge plasma, the pressure tensor is generally anisotropic, so \(p_{\parallel,s}\) differs from the perpendicular pressure \(p_{\perp,s}\); using the isotropic scalar pressure \(p_s\) is only valid in the limit of weak anisotropy.

Sign convention: Positive when the net momentum flux is directed in the direction of the local magnetic field unit vector \(\hat{b}\) (i.e., in the direction of increasing field-line arc length along \(\hat{b}\)).

This quantity is stored as a GGD (Generalized Grid Description) scalar field at the locations defined by the GGD grid subset, with one value per grid element. The corresponding data dictionary path is edge_transport/model/ggd/ion/state/momentum/flux_parallel/values in the edge_transport IDS.

Typical magnitude ranges in edge plasmas vary widely with plasma conditions: from approximately \(10^{-2}\) kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\) in cold, low-density divertor detachment conditions up to \(\sim 10^1\) kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\) in hot attached scrape-off-layer plasmas. The ion charge state index distinguishes contributions from different ionization states of a given ion species, enabling detailed multi-fluid transport modeling.

The parallel momentum flux is a key quantity in edge transport models, governing the parallel flow of ions along field lines toward divertor targets and playing a central role in momentum balance equations that determine the plasma flow profile in the scrape-off layer.

Unit: kg.m^-1.s^-2

Kind: scalar

Status: Draft

docs.title: parallel_component_of_neutral_momentum_flux
docs.text:
Field-aligned component of the momentum flux carried by neutral particles in the edge plasma, summed over all neutral species. Includes both convective (ram pressure) and kinetic pressure contributions along the magnetic field direction. Sourced from the edge_transport IDS at edge_transport/model/ggd/neutral/momentum/flux_parallel/values.

The parallel neutral momentum flux \(\Pi_{\parallel,\mathrm{n}}\) is the projection of the neutral-species momentum flux tensor onto the local magnetic field direction \(\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|\). It is defined as the sum over all neutral species \(s\):

\[\Pi_{\parallel,\mathrm{n}} = \sum_s \left( m_s n_s v_{\parallel,s}^2 + p_s \right)\]

where \(m_s\) is the species mass (kg), \(n_s\) is the number density (m\(^{-3}\)), \(v_{\parallel,s} = \mathbf{v}_s \cdot \hat{b}\) is the field-aligned flow velocity (m s\(^{-1}\)), and \(p_s\) is the scalar (isotropic) pressure of species \(s\) (Pa = kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\)). Because neutrals carry no net charge, each species \(s\) here refers to a distinct neutral atom or molecule type, not a charge state; the phrase "neutral charge states" does not apply. The pressure term \(p_s\) is taken as the scalar isotropic pressure, which is appropriate for neutral particles in the collisional edge plasma where velocity distributions are approximately Maxwellian.

The quantity is defined on a General Grid Description (GGD) subset of the computational mesh inside the edge_transport IDS (path: edge_transport/model/ggd/neutral/momentum/flux_parallel/values). One scalar value is provided per mesh element in the relevant grid subset.

Sign convention: Positive when the net momentum flux is directed along the direction of the magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) (i.e., in the direction of increasing arc length along field lines from low to high toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame).

Typical magnitudes in the edge plasma range from \(\sim 10^{-2}\) to \(\sim 10^{2}\) kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\) depending on neutral density, species (hydrogen isotopes, helium, impurities), and plasma conditions (attached vs.~detached divertor regimes). Near the divertor target in high-recycling conditions, neutral ram pressure can approach or exceed ion parallel momentum flux, making this quantity important for momentum balance in detachment modeling.

This quantity appears in the neutral fluid momentum equation and is used in edge transport codes (e.g., SOLPS-ITER, EDGE2D-EIRENE) to close the parallel momentum balance for the neutral fluid. It is distinct from the total (ion + neutral) parallel momentum flux and from the parallel ion momentum flux.

docs.title: parallel_component_of_neutral_state_momentum_flux
docs.text:
Projection of the momentum flux tensor for a kinetically resolved neutral charge state onto the local magnetic field direction, quantifying field-aligned neutral momentum transport in the edge plasma.

The parallel component of the neutral-state momentum flux \(\Pi_{\parallel,ns}\) represents the rate of momentum transport per unit area carried by a specific neutral charge state (e.g., a particular ionization stage of a hydrogen or impurity neutral) along the direction of the local magnetic field \(\hat{b}\). It is defined as \(\Pi_{\parallel,ns} = \hat{b} \cdot \overleftrightarrow{\Pi}_{ns} \cdot \hat{b}\), where \(\overleftrightarrow{\Pi}_{ns} = m_{ns} n_{ns} \mathbf{v}_{ns} \mathbf{v}_{ns} + p_{ns} \overleftrightarrow{I}\) is the momentum flux tensor of the resolved neutral state, \(m_{ns}\) is the particle mass, \(n_{ns}\) is the number density, \(\mathbf{v}_{ns}\) is the fluid velocity, and \(p_{ns}\) is the partial pressure. Resolving individual neutral charge states rather than the aggregate neutral population—as in parallel_component_of_neutral_momentum_flux—enables state-specific collisional source terms and charge-exchange rates to be evaluated accurately in multi-fluid edge codes. This quantity is the neutral-state analog of parallel_component_of_ion_state_momentum_flux, and both are typically computed by fluid or kinetic-fluid edge transport codes (e.g., Monte Carlo neutral solvers coupled to fluid plasma models) operating on the unstructured GGD mesh. The parent tensor quantity is neutral_state_momentum_flux, while the species-aggregated parallel limit is parallel_component_of_momentum_flux. Typical magnitudes in the divertor region range from \(10^{1}\) to \(10^{4}\) kg m\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\), depending on neutral density and temperature.

Unit: kg.m^-1.s^-2

docs.title: parallel_component_of_total_momentum_flux
docs.text:
Parallel (field-aligned) component of the total plasma momentum flux, summing contributions from all carrier species including ions and neutrals, representing the net field-aligned rate of momentum transport per unit area across surfaces in the edge plasma.

The parallel component of the total momentum flux is the projection of the combined plasma momentum flux tensor onto the local magnetic field direction \(\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|\). For a multi-species plasma it is defined as \(\Pi_\parallel = \hat{b} \cdot \left(\sum_s \mathbf{\Pi}_s\right) \cdot \hat{b}\), where \(\mathbf{\Pi}_s = m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s \mathbf{v}_s + p_s \mathbf{I}\) is the momentum flux tensor for species \(s\) (with \(m_s\) the particle mass, \(n_s\) the number density, \(\mathbf{v}_s\) the fluid velocity, and \(p_s\) the scalar pressure), summed over all ion charge states and neutral populations. This aggregate quantity differs from parallel_component_of_ion_state_momentum_flux and parallel_component_of_neutral_momentum_flux, which resolve individual carriers; it also differs from parallel_component_of_momentum_flux, which may exclude certain neutral contributions depending on the model closure. In edge transport simulations the parallel momentum flux governs the flow of momentum along open field lines toward material surfaces and sets the parallel flow velocity boundary condition at the divertor target. Typical magnitudes in the scrape-off layer range from \(10^2\) to \(10^4\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}\) depending on upstream density, temperature, and plasma-facing-component geometry. The quantity is evaluated on the GGD unstructured edge grid, with one value per grid element in the relevant grid subset. Related vector-form quantities are given by momentum_flux, and the vertical projection is captured by vertical_component_of_momentum_flux.

docs.title: maximum_magnetic_field_strength_on_flux_surface
docs.text: Maximum of the total magnetic field modulus |B| taken over all points on each flux surface, yielding a positive-definite scalar for each surface label. This quantity enters neoclassical transport theory and determines the threshold pitch angle for magnetically trapped particles.

docs.title: Maximum Magnetic Field Strength on Flux Surface
docs.text:
For a given flux surface labeled by a normalized flux coordinate (e.g., \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_{\mathrm{boundary}}}\), where \(\Phi\) is the toroidal magnetic flux), this quantity is defined as

\[B_{\max}(\rho) = \sup_{\theta,\phi}\, |\mathbf{B}(R(\rho,\theta,\phi),\,\phi,\,Z(\rho,\theta,\phi))|,\]

where the supremum is taken over all poloidal angles \(\theta\) and toroidal angles \(\phi\) on the surface, and \(|\mathbf{B}|\) is evaluated in the right-handed cylindrical \((R,\phi,Z)\) frame. The result is always strictly positive regardless of the sign convention applied to individual magnetic field components.

Physical context. In an axisymmetric tokamak the toroidal dependence drops out and the maximum is attained at the high-field side (small \(R\)), where the dominant toroidal field component \(B_\phi \sim B_0 R_0 / R\) is largest. Typical values in conventional tokamaks range from roughly 3 T on axis to 6–10 T at the high-field side for high-field devices.

\(B_{\max}\) together with \(B_{\min}\) (the minimum on the same surface) determines the local mirror ratio \(R_{\mathrm{mirror}} = B_{\max}/B_{\min}\), which governs the fraction of magnetically trapped particles. A particle with velocity-space pitch angle \(\lambda = v_\perp^2 / (v^2 B)\) satisfies the trapping condition when \(\lambda > 1/B_{\max}\), i.e., when its magnetic moment prevents it from passing through the field maximum. This in turn controls neoclassical transport coefficients such as the bootstrap current and thermal conductivity.

IMAS data dictionary provenance. This standard name maps to equilibrium/time_slice/profiles_1d/b_field_max (Maximum(modulus(B)) on the flux surface, always positive) in the equilibrium IDS. A closely related path equilibrium/time_slice/profiles_1d/b_max stores Maximum(B) on the flux surface and may differ in treatment of field-direction sign. Both paths are indexed along the same 1D flux-surface grid as other profiles_1d quantities.

Sign convention: Positive definite; \(B_{\max}\) is the modulus and carries no sign.

Unit: T

Kind: scalar

docs.title: toroidal_component_of_shattered_pellet_velocity
docs.text:
Projection of the shattered pellet injector (SPI) pellet center-of-mass velocity onto the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

The toroidal velocity component \(v_\phi\) quantifies how fast the SPI pellet's center-of-mass moves along the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\) as it travels through the plasma vessel before and during the shattering event. It is the \(\hat{\phi}\)-projection of the full velocity vector described by shattered_pellet_velocity, i.e. \(v_\phi = \mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{\phi}\), where \(\hat{\phi}\) points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\). In most SPI configurations the pellet is injected with predominantly radial or vertical motion and the toroidal component is small (typically \(|v_\phi| \ll |v_R|\)), but finite toroidal injection angles are used on some devices to optimize material deposition for disruption mitigation. This component is inferred from pellet-tracking diagnostics (e.g. fast cameras, pellet-imaging systems) or from the known injector geometry and pellet speed measured before shattering; consult shattered_pellet_speed_before_shattering for the pre-shattering speed magnitude. The complementary spatial components are the major-radius component radial_component_of_shattered_pellet_velocity and the vertical component vertical_component_of_shattered_pellet_fragment_cloud_velocity for the post-shattering fragment cloud.

Sign convention: Positive when \(v_\phi\) points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\) (counter-clockwise when viewed from above \(+\hat{Z}\)).

docs.title: area_of_flux_loop
docs.text:
Effective sensing area of a flux loop diagnostic, defined as the ratio of the measured magnetic flux to the mean magnetic field over the loop aperture. This geometric property governs the flux linkage sensitivity of the loop and is used to convert induced voltage signals into magnetic flux measurements.

The effective area \(A\) of a flux loop is defined by \(\Phi = A \langle B_n \rangle\), where \(\Phi\) is the total magnetic flux threading the loop and \(\langle B_n \rangle\) is the average normal component of the magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) over the loop aperture. For an ideal planar single-turn loop, \(A\) equals the geometric enclosed area; for multi-turn or non-planar geometries, \(A\) represents the effective flux-collection area accounting for the coil winding geometry. This quantity is undefined (and should be left empty) when the flux loop is configured as a differential loop (type index 6), since differential loops measure field gradients rather than total flux.

The effective area is determined during in-situ calibration or from engineering drawings, and typical values range from a few \(\text{cm}^2\) to several hundred \(\text{cm}^2\) depending on the loop size and machine geometry. Compared to the cross-sectional area of a poloidal magnetic field probe or the cross-sectional area of a Rogowski coil, which characterize per-turn winding geometry, the flux loop effective area characterizes the total flux-collecting aperture of the full loop diagnostic.

Sign convention: Positive when the flux through the loop is in the direction consistent with the right-hand rule applied to the loop's defined normal vector in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

docs.title: radial_component_of_ferritic_element_magnetic_moment
docs.text:
Radial (\(\hat{R}\)) component of the magnetic dipole moment per unit area induced in a ferritic structural element by the ambient tokamak magnetic field, representing the magnetization state projected onto the major-radius direction.

The radial component \(M_R = \mathbf{M} \cdot \hat{R}\) isolates the magnetization of ferritic structural elements — such as ferritic steel test blanket modules or vacuum vessel segments — along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. Ferritic components become magnetized through their nonlinear permeability response to the local field \(\mathbf{B}\), and the resulting induced moment density modifies the equilibrium field distribution, particularly near the plasma boundary. Together with toroidal_component_of_ferritic_element_magnetic_moment and vertical_component_of_ferritic_element_magnetic_moment, this quantity completes the cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) decomposition of ferritic_element_magnetic_moment. The radial component is typically the smallest of the three cylindrical components in axisymmetric configurations where \(B_\phi\) dominates, but becomes significant near non-axisymmetric features or during transients. It is computed from finite-element or boundary-element magnetostatic models of the ferritic structure driven by the reconstructed plasma and coil fields.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetization component points in the direction of increasing major radius \(R\) (outward from the machine symmetry axis).

docs.text:
Projection of the shattered pellet injector (SPI) pellet center-of-mass velocity onto the major-radius direction \(R\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, isolating the inward or outward radial motion of the pellet.

The radial velocity component \(v_R\) is the \(R\)-projection of the full pellet center-of-mass velocity vector described by shattered_pellet_velocity, decomposed as \(v_R = \mathbf{v} \cdot \hat{R}\), where \(\hat{R}\) points away from the machine symmetry axis. docs.text:
Toroidal angle φ of the first endpoint defining the line of sight of a diagnostic channel, specifying the azimuthal entry point of the chord in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

docs.title: vertical_component_of_center_of_mass_velocity
docs.text:
Projection of the mass-weighted mean fluid velocity of the plasma mixture onto the vertical Z-axis of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, representing the net upward or downward bulk motion of all species combined.

The vertical component of the center-of-mass velocity is defined as \(v_{Z,\mathrm{cm}} = \hat{Z} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cm}}\), where the center-of-mass velocity \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{cm}} = \sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s / \sum_s m_s n_s\) is the mass-density-weighted mean velocity summed over all species \(s\) (electrons, ions, neutrals), with \(m_s\) the species mass, \(n_s\) the number density, and \(\mathbf{v}_s\) the species fluid velocity. This quantity is the \(Z\)-component of center_of_mass_velocity and differs from individual-species vertical velocities such as vertical_component_of_ion_velocity or vertical_component_of_neutral_velocity in that it accounts for the full momentum budget of the mixture rather than a single species. It appears in the continuity and total-momentum equations of multi-fluid transport models and is relevant to impurity transport, divertor target loads, and vertical stability analysis. Typical magnitudes range from a few m/s in quiescent edge plasmas to tens of km/s during disruptions or ELMs. It is computed from multi-fluid simulation codes or inferred by combining charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy data for multiple ion species with electron measurements weighted by their respective mass densities.

Sign convention: Positive when \(v_{Z,\mathrm{cm}}\) points in the direction of increasing \(Z\) (upward, away from the divertor in standard lower-single-null configurations).

docs.title: co_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion
docs.text:
Volumetric power density received by the co-passing fast particle population from bulk ions via Coulomb collisions, quantifying the aggregate ion-to-fast-particle energy exchange rate for the co-passing orbit-class fraction of the non-thermal distribution.

This quantity gives the collisional power density \(P_{\rm coll}\) (in \(\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\)) exchanged between the bulk ion population (all charge states summed) and the co-passing subset of the fast (suprathermal) particle distribution through binary Coulomb collisions. Co-passing fast particles are those whose guiding-center motion circulates toroidally in the same direction as the net plasma current, tracing untrapped orbits that encircle the torus poloidally. The exchange rate is governed by the Fokker–Planck collision operator \(C(f_{\rm fast}, f_{\rm ion})\), where the power density is \(P_{\rm coll} = \int m_f v^2 / 2 \, C(f_{\rm fast}, f_{\rm ion})\, d^3v\), with \(m_f\) the fast-particle mass and \(v\) the particle speed. Positive values indicate net energy transfer from bulk ions to the co-passing fast particles; negative values indicate net fast-particle slowing-down energy deposited into the ions. This quantity is computed by fast-particle Monte Carlo or Fokker–Planck codes (e.g. TRANSP, ASCOT, ICRH/NBI Fokker–Planck solvers) that resolve the orbit-class decomposition of the distribution function. Typical magnitudes in neutral-beam or ICRH-heated tokamak discharges range from \(10^4\) to \(10^7\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\) in the plasma core, depending on fast-particle density and bulk ion temperature. The aggregate-ion counterpart for the counter-passing orbit class is counter_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion. When charge-state resolution is required, the companion quantity co_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion_state resolves the same exchange at the level of individual ionic charge states. The electron-channel analog is co_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_electrons. Summing over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped orbit classes recovers the total fast_particle_collisional_power_density_to_thermal_ion.

docs.title: counter_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion
docs.text:
Volumetric power density received by the counter-passing fast particle population from bulk ions via Coulomb collisions. Positive values indicate net energy transfer from ions to the counter-passing fast particles. This scalar represents the collisional energy exchange rate per unit volume for the counter-passing orbit class.

The quantity \(P_{\rm cp,fast\leftarrow ion}\) is the net collisional power density received by the counter-passing fast particle population from the bulk ion species through Coulomb collisions, integrated over the counter-passing velocity-space domain and over all contributing ion species:

\[P_{\rm cp,fast\leftarrow ion} = \int_{\rm cp} C[f_{\rm fast}, f_i]\, E\, d^3v\]

where \(C[f_{\rm fast}, f_i]\) is the Coulomb collision operator coupling the fast particle distribution \(f_{\rm fast}\) to the bulk ion distribution \(f_i\), and \(E\) is the particle kinetic energy.

The counter-passing orbit class consists of fast particles whose parallel velocity component is directed opposite to the toroidal magnetic field direction (i.e., in the \(-\hat{\phi}\) direction of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame).

Sign convention: Positive when net energy flows from the bulk ions into the counter-passing fast particle population (ions lose energy, fast particles gain energy).

Typical values range from \(10^3\) to \(10^7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\) in high-power heating scenarios (NBI, ICRF), and may be negative when the fast particles are slowing down and transferring energy back to the thermal ions.

This quantity is stored in the IMAS data dictionary at distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/counter_passing/collisions/ion/power_fast and distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/counter_passing/collisions/ion/power_fast, under the distributions IDS.

docs.title: trapped_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_to_thermal_electron
docs.text: Volumetric power density deposited into the thermal electron population via Coulomb collisions with trapped fast (non-thermal) particles. This is the locally evaluated energy exchange rate per unit volume attributable exclusively to the trapped-orbit subset of the fast-particle distribution, and is positive when net energy flows from fast particles to thermal electrons.

docs.title: Trapped Fast-Particle Collisional Power Density to Thermal Electrons
Physical definition
docs.text:
This quantity gives the local volumetric power density \(Q_{\mathrm{trap},e}^{\mathrm{coll}}\) (units: \(\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\)) transferred from the trapped-orbit subset of the fast-particle distribution to the thermal electron population through Coulomb collisions (electron drag and pitch-angle scattering). It is defined as

\[Q_{\mathrm{trap},e}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathrm{trapped}} u_{se}(v)\, E_k\, f_f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v})\, d^3v,\]

where the integration is restricted to trapped-orbit phase-space (i.e., particles whose guiding-center bounce trajectory does not complete a full toroidal transit), $ u_{se}(v)$ is the velocity-dependent slowing-down frequency on electrons, \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}m_f v^2\) is the fast-particle kinetic energy, and \(f_f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v})\) is the fast-particle distribution function in units of \(\mathrm{m^{-6}\,s^3}\) (number of particles per unit phase-space volume). The integral therefore carries units of \(\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\) — power per unit real-space volume, evaluated at position \(\mathbf{x}\) in the IMAS cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame.

docs.title: Orbit-class partitioning
docs.text: The trapped subset is distinguished from the passing subsets (co-passing and counter-passing) by the trapping condition on the pitch-angle variable \(\xi = v_\parallel / v\): a particle at position \(\mathbf{x}\) is classified as trapped when \(|\xi| < \xi_{\mathrm{trap}}(\mathbf{x})\), where \(\xi_{\mathrm{trap}} = \sqrt{1 - B(\mathbf{x})/B_{\mathrm{max}}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{max}}\) is the maximum magnetic field along the flux surface. Summing the trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing contributions exactly reconstructs the total collisional power density to thermal electrons: \(Q_{\mathrm{total},e}^{\mathrm{coll}} = Q_{\mathrm{trap},e}^{\mathrm{coll}} + Q_{\mathrm{co},e}^{\mathrm{coll}} + Q_{\mathrm{ctr},e}^{\mathrm{coll}}\).

docs.title: Sign convention
docs.text: Sign convention: Positive when net energy flows from the trapped fast-particle population into the thermal electrons (heating). A negative value would indicate anomalous back-transfer, which is unphysical under classical Coulomb collisions but may appear as a numerical artifact.

docs.title: IMAS / DD provenance
docs.text:
This scalar is sourced from the IMAS distributions IDS at the path

distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/trapped/collisions/electrons/power_thermal

(unit: \(\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\), annotated as "Collisional power density to the thermal particle population"). The trapped node in the DD path explicitly identifies the orbit-class; the sibling nodes co_passing and counter_passing hold the corresponding passing-orbit contributions.

docs.title: Typical values and context
docs.text:
In NBI- or ICRH-heated tokamak plasmas, the total fast-electron collisional power density peaks on axis at \(10^3\)–\(10^6\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}\) depending on heating power and plasma density. The trapped fraction depends strongly on inverse aspect ratio \(\epsilon = r/R\): at low \(\epsilon\) the trapped fraction \(f_{\mathrm{trap}} \approx 2\sqrt{\epsilon}\) is small, while near the plasma edge it can approach 50 %. Consequently \(Q_{\mathrm{trap},e}^{\mathrm{coll}}\) is typically smaller than the co-passing contribution on axis but becomes comparable at mid-radius and beyond.

This quantity is used in transport solvers (e.g., as a source term in the electron energy equation) and in RF/NBI power balance analysis.

docs.title: co_passing_fast_particle_collisional_power_density_to_thermal_ion
docs.text:
Volumetric power density transferred from co-passing fast particles to bulk thermal ions via Coulomb collisions. One of three orbit-class contributions (co-passing, counter-passing, trapped) to the total fast-particle-to-ion collisional heating source.

This quantity is the collisional power density delivered to the bulk thermal ion population by the co-passing orbit-class subset of the fast-particle distribution. It is one of three orbit-class components — co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped — that together constitute the total fast-particle-to-thermal-ion heating source term in the ion energy balance equation.

Physical definition: the power per unit volume transferred from co-passing fast particles to thermal ions through Coulomb friction and diffusion. For a species \(s\) of fast ions with distribution function \(f_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{v})\) normalized such that \(\int f_{\mathrm{co}}\,d^3v\) gives the co-passing fast-ion number density (m\(^{-3}\)), the quantity is

\[P_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{th\,ion}} = \int u_{\mathrm{si}}(v)\,E_k\,\mathcal{T}_{i}\{f_{\mathrm{co}}\}\,d^3v \quad [\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}]\]

where $ u_{\mathrm{si}}(v)$ is the velocity-dependent slowing-down frequency on thermal ions, \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}m_s v^2\) is the fast-particle kinetic energy, and \(\mathcal{T}_{i}\{f_{\mathrm{co}}\}\) is the ion-channel Fokker–Planck collision operator acting on \(f_{\mathrm{co}}\), which distributes the transferred energy exclusively to the thermal ion population. The integral is restricted to the co-passing velocity-space domain (\(v_\parallel > 0\), \(|v_\parallel/v| > \lambda_{\mathrm{T/P}}\), where \(\lambda_{\mathrm{T/P}}\) is the trapped–passing boundary).

Typical values in neutral-beam-heated tokamak plasmas range from \(10^3\) to \(10^6\) W m\(^{-3}\), depending on fast-ion density, beam energy, and plasma temperature.

Sign convention: Positive when energy flows from the co-passing fast particles to the thermal ion population, corresponding to net heating of the ions.

In the IMAS data dictionary this quantity is stored under distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/co_passing/collisions/ion/power_thermal (IDS: distributions, unit: W m\(^{-3}\)). The full thermal-ion heating source is recovered by summing the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions over all fast-particle species.

docs.title: fast_particle_collisional_power_density_to_thermal_ion
docs.text:
Volumetric power density transferred from the total fast (suprathermal) particle population to bulk thermal ions via Coulomb collisions, summed over all orbit classes (co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped).

This quantity gives the net collisional energy exchange rate per unit volume from the entire fast-particle distribution — encompassing co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped orbit classes — to the bulk thermal ion population. It appears as a source term \(S_{fi}\) in the ion energy balance equation

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac{3}{2} n_i T_i\right) + abla \cdot \mathbf{q}_i = S_{fi} + \ldots\]

where \(n_i\) is the thermal ion density, \(T_i\) is the thermal ion temperature, and \(\mathbf{q}_i\) is the ion heat flux. The exchange rate arises from Coulomb drag: energetic particles slow down on the background plasma, depositing power preferentially to ions when the fast-particle velocity \(v_f\) is below the critical slowing-down velocity \(v_c \approx (3\sqrt{\pi}/4)^{1/3}(m_i/m_e)^{1/6}v_{\mathrm{th},e}\), where \(m_i\) and \(m_e\) are the ion and electron masses and \(v_{\mathrm{th},e}\) is the electron thermal velocity.

In neutral-beam-injected or ICRH-heated plasmas, this power density governs the fraction of auxiliary heating that goes to the ions rather than electrons; typical values range from \(10^5\) to \(10^8\) W m\(^{-3}\) in the core of medium-to-large tokamaks. It is computed from Fokker–Planck or Monte Carlo distribution-function codes applied to the fast-particle distribution function \(f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})\).

Orbit-class-resolved contributions are captured by co-passing fast particle collisional power density to thermal ion and counter-passing fast particle collisional power density to thermal ion, while trapped fast particle collisional power density transferred to thermal ions covers the trapped sub-population. The analogous transfer to the electron channel is described by fast particle collisional power density due to Coulomb collisions with electrons. For the charge-state-resolved version, see fast particle collisional power density to thermal ion state due to Coulomb collisions.

docs.title: Trapped Fast-Particle Collisional Power Density to Thermal Ions
docs.text:
This quantity is the local volumetric rate at which energy is transferred from the trapped suprathermal (fast) particle population to the thermal ion fluid through Coulomb collisions. It is defined as the velocity-space moment of the collisional energy-exchange operator \(C[f_\mathrm{fast}]\) weighted by the particle kinetic energy \(\tfrac{1}{2}m v^2\):

\[p_\mathrm{coll} = \int \frac{1}{2}m v^2\, C[f_\mathrm{fast}, f_\mathrm{ion}]\, d^3v \quad [\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}]\]

where \(f_\mathrm{fast}\) is the trapped fast-particle distribution function, \(f_\mathrm{ion}\) is the thermal ion distribution function, and the integral is performed over the trapped portion of velocity space. The result is a scalar field resolved locally in the plasma volume (or along a flux-surface-averaged profile, depending on the IDS context), stored with units W m\(^{-3}\).

In the slowing-down picture, energy is transferred from suprathermal particles to the thermal ions at a rate proportional to the ion-drag friction force \(F_\mathrm{drag}^\mathrm{ion}(v)\) integrated over the fast-particle velocity distribution. The fraction of power deposited on ions (as opposed to electrons) depends strongly on the fast-particle injection energy relative to the critical energy \(E_c = \tfrac{1}{2}m_f v_c^2\), where \(v_c\) is the critical velocity separating ion-dominated and electron-dominated slowing-down regimes. For \(E_\mathrm{fast} \gg E_c\), the majority of fast-particle energy flows to electrons; for \(E_\mathrm{fast} \ll E_c\), energy flows predominantly to ions.

Typical values in reactor-relevant scenarios range from \(10^4\) to \(10^7\) W m\(^{-3}\), depending on plasma density, fast-particle source strength (e.g., neutral beam or fusion alpha), and radial location.

This quantity is sourced from the distributions IDS, specifically from: - distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/trapped/collisions/ion/power_thermal (flux-surface-averaged profile, W m\(^{-3}\)) - distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/trapped/collisions/ion/power_thermal (2-D poloidal-plane resolved, W m\(^{-3}\))

docs.title: fast_particle_density
docs.text:
Number density of fast (suprathermal) particles on a given flux surface, summed over all orbit classes and velocity-space pitch angles, representing the total non-thermal contribution to the local particle inventory.

The fast-particle number density \(n_\mathrm{fast}\) is defined as the zeroth velocity-space moment of the suprathermal distribution function \(f_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{v})\), integrated over all velocities above the suprathermal threshold \(v_\mathrm{th,cut}\) and over all pitch angles \(\xi = v_\parallel/v\):

\[n_\mathrm{fast} = \int_{v > v_\mathrm{th,cut}} \int_{-1}^{1} f_\mathrm{fast}(v, \xi)\, 2\pi v^2\, d\xi\, dv\]

The quantity reported on a flux surface is the flux-surface average

\[\langle n_\mathrm{fast} \rangle = \frac{\oint n_\mathrm{fast}\, dA / | abla \psi|}{\oint dA / | abla \psi|}\]

where the surface integral is taken at constant normalized poloidal flux \(\psi\).

The suprathermal threshold \(v_\mathrm{th,cut}\) is typically defined as a multiple of the local thermal speed \(v_\mathrm{th} = \sqrt{2 k_B T / m}\), often taken as \(v_\mathrm{th,cut} \approx 2\text{--}3\, v_\mathrm{th}\), but its precise definition is model- and code-dependent. When the fast-particle population is anisotropic (e.g., beam-injected ions or ICRH-heated minority species), the threshold should be understood as applying to the total speed \(v = |\mathbf{v}|\) and includes contributions from all pitch angles; no assumption of isotropy is made.

Typical values range from \(\sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) for weakly heated discharges to \(\sim 10^{18}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) in strongly NBI- or ICRH-driven plasmas. Fast particles from fusion-born alpha particles contribute at the upper end of this range in burning plasmas.

This quantity is non-negative by definition (it is a number density).

docs.title: trapped_fast_particle_density
docs.text:
Number density of fast (suprathermal) particles on trapped orbits, representing only the fraction of the non-thermal distribution whose velocity-space pitch angle places them in the magnetically trapped orbit class.

Trapped fast particles occupy velocity-space regions where \(v_\parallel / v < \sqrt{1 - B_{\min}/B_{\max}}\), with \(v_\parallel\) the velocity component parallel to the local magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\), \(B_{\min}\) and \(B_{\max}\) the minimum and maximum field strengths along the field line. These particles execute banana orbits rather than passing orbits, and their density \(n_{\mathrm{trap,fast}}\) is obtained by integrating the fast-particle distribution function \(f(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})\) over the trapped portion of velocity space: \(n_{\mathrm{trap,fast}} = \int_{\mathrm{trapped}} f\, d^3v\). The trapped fast population is particularly relevant to neoclassical transport, bootstrap current generation, and the resonant drive of energetic-particle modes such as toroidal Alfven eigenmodes (TAEs). Typical values range from \(10^{16}\) to \(10^{19}\) m\(^{-3}\) depending on plasma scenario and neutral beam or radio-frequency heating power. The trapped fraction is computed from kinetic distribution solvers (e.g., Monte Carlo or Fokker-Planck codes) applied to neutral beam injection or ICRH fast-ion sources. It complements co-passing fast particle density and counter-passing fast particle density, which together with this quantity partition fast_particle_density by orbit class. The corresponding all-energy (thermal plus non-thermal) trapped population is described by trapped_particle_density.

Sign convention: Positive when the number density of trapped fast particles is greater than zero, i.e. when the trapped fast-particle population is present in the plasma.

docs.title: trapped_particle_density
docs.text: Total number density of particles — thermal plus non-thermal — whose parallel velocity is small enough that the magnetic mirror force confines them to a bounded poloidal arc rather than allowing full poloidal transit. Equivalently, these are particles with pitch angle exceeding the local trapping criterion defined by the magnetic field variation on a flux surface.

docs.title: Trapped Particle Density
docs.text:
The trapped particle density \(n_\mathrm{trap}\) is the total number of trapped-orbit particles (thermal and non-thermal) per unit volume on a given flux surface. A particle is classified as trapped when its pitch angle \(\lambda = v_\parallel / v\) satisfies the local mirror trapping condition

\[|v_\parallel| < v \sqrt{1 - B_\mathrm{min}/B}\]

where \(B\) is the local magnetic field magnitude and \(B_\mathrm{min}\) is the minimum field on the same flux surface. Such particles undergo bounce oscillations between mirror points and do not complete full poloidal circuits.

The quantity is resolved on flux surfaces and stored as a function of the minor-radial coordinate (typically \(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}\), the normalized toroidal flux radius) and optionally on a two-dimensional \((R, Z)\) poloidal grid in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame where \(R\) is the major radius, \(\phi\) is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and \(Z\) is the vertical height. It is NOT a bounce-averaged quantity; it represents the local particle density integrated over the trapped portion of velocity space at each spatial point.

The orbit-class partition identity reads

\[n_\mathrm{total} = n_\mathrm{trap} + n_\mathrm{co} + n_\mathrm{counter}\]

where \(n_\mathrm{co}\) and \(n_\mathrm{counter}\) are the co-passing and counter-passing densities respectively.

Typical values: In a deuterium plasma with \(n_e \sim 10^{19}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) and inverse aspect ratio \(\epsilon = r/R \sim 0.1\)–\(0.3\), the trapped fraction \(f_t \approx 1.46\sqrt{\epsilon} - 0.46\epsilon\) implies \(n_\mathrm{trap} \sim (0.3\)–\(0.6)\,n_\mathrm{total}\).

IMAS/DD source paths: - distributions/distribution/profiles_1d/trapped/density (m\(^{-3}\), thermal+non-thermal) - distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/trapped/density (m\(^{-3}\), thermal+non-thermal)

Physical context: Trapped particles drive neoclassical transport through banana-regime diffusion and are responsible for bootstrap current generation. Their density appears directly in neoclassical transport coefficients and in gyrokinetic stability calculations for drift-wave and kinetic-ballooning instabilities.

docs.title: vertical_component_of_e_cross_b_drift_velocity
docs.text:
Vertical Z-component of the E×B drift velocity for charged plasma species in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z is the vertical height axis. The drift arises from crossed electric and magnetic fields and acts on ions and electrons but not on neutral particles. One scalar value is stored per grid-subset element in the GGD representation.

The E×B drift velocity is given by

\[\mathbf{v}_{E\times B} = \frac{\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}}{|B|^2}\]

where \(\mathbf{E}\) is the electric field vector and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the magnetic field vector. This standard name records the projection of that velocity onto the vertical \(\hat{Z}\) axis of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, i.e.

\[v_{E\times B,Z} = \frac{(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{Z}}{|B|^2} = \frac{E_R B_\phi - E_\phi B_R}{|B|^2}\]

where \(E_R\), \(E_\phi\) are the radial and toroidal components of the electric field and \(B_R\), \(B_\phi\) are the corresponding magnetic field components in the \((R, \phi, Z)\) basis.

This drift acts on all charged species (ions and electrons) but does not apply to neutral particles, which are unaffected by electromagnetic forces. Neutral velocity components along \(Z\) are separately described by convective or pressure-driven transport.

Typical magnitudes in tokamak edge and scrape-off-layer regions range from \(10^2\) to \(10^4\) m/s, depending on the local electric field strength and magnetic field magnitude.

In the IMAS data dictionary this quantity is stored at paths such as plasma_profiles/ggd/ion/state/velocity_exb/z and plasma_profiles/ggd/neutral/state/velocity_exb/z, where each element corresponds to one cell or node in the associated GGD grid subset (one scalar value per element).

Sign convention: Positive when the E×B drift points in the direction of increasing \(Z\) (upward, i.e., away from the midplane toward the top of the vessel).

Kind: scalar

docs.title: poloidal_component_of_electric_field
docs.text:
Projection of the plasma electric field onto the local poloidal direction, defined as the dot product of the electric field vector with the poloidal unit vector at each point on a flux surface. This component appears in the poloidal projection of the generalized Ohm's law and in flux-surface-averaged force balance along the poloidal direction.

The poloidal component of the electric field is defined by

\[E_\theta = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\theta}\]

where \(\hat{\theta}\) is the unit vector in the poloidal direction, tangent to the flux surface and lying in the meridional \((R, Z)\) plane of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. Note that \(\hat{\theta}\) is not a basis vector of the cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame; it is defined by the geometry of the specific flux surface and the choice of poloidal angle \(\theta\) increasing counter-clockwise in the \((R, Z)\) poloidal cross-section when viewed with \(\phi\) increasing out of the page.

In the poloidal projection of the generalized Ohm's law, \(E_\theta\) balances resistive, inductive, and electron-pressure-gradient contributions. It participates in the parallel electric field through the decomposition \(E_\parallel = E_\theta \sin\alpha + E_\phi \cos\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the pitch angle of the magnetic field.

Typical values: In a standard tokamak discharge, \(|E_\theta|\) is typically in the range \(10^{-3}\)–\(10^{-1}\) V m\(^{-1}\) in the bulk plasma, with larger values possible near transport barriers or during transient events.

Units: V m\(^{-1}\) (stored as V.m^-1 in the IMAS data dictionary).

Sign convention: Positive when the electric field vector points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle \(\theta\), where \(\theta\) increases counter-clockwise in the \((R, Z)\) poloidal cross-section.

docs.title: radial_component_of_electric_field
docs.text:
Component of the plasma electric field along the major-radius direction R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the projection E_R = E · R-hat, obtained from the negative radial gradient of the electrostatic potential. This component drives cross-field drifts and is central to radial force balance in magnetized plasmas.

The radial electric field \(E_R\) is the component of the total electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) along the major-radius unit vector \(\hat{R}\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and \(Z\) is the vertical height.

It is defined by the projection

\[E_R = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{R} = -\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial R},\]

where \(\Phi\) is the electrostatic potential. This quantity is stored in the IMAS IDS at core_profiles/profiles_1d/e_field/radial and is typically provided as a function of a radial flux-surface coordinate such as \(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}\) (normalized toroidal flux radius).

Note that in a general shaped equilibrium, the direction \(\hat{R}\) is not identical to the direction perpendicular to a flux surface; the flux-surface-normal direction acquires contributions from both \(\hat{R}\) and \(\hat{Z}\). The quantity \(E_R\) therefore represents the laboratory-frame cylindrical projection and should not be equated directly with the flux-surface-perpendicular electric field \(E_\perp\) except in the limit of circular, concentric flux surfaces.

Radial force balance. For a given ion species \(s\) with charge \(q_s\), the radial force-balance relation reads

\[q_s E_R = \frac{1}{n_s}\frac{\partial p_s}{\partial R} - v_{\phi,s} B_Z + v_{Z,s} B_\phi,\]

where \(n_s\) is the species density, \(p_s\) is the pressure, and \(v_{\phi,s}\), \(v_{Z,s}\) are the toroidal and vertical flow components respectively, with \(B_\phi\) and \(B_Z\) the corresponding magnetic-field components.

\(E\times B\) rotation. The \(E\times B\) drift velocity in the poloidal plane, which drives toroidal plasma rotation, involves a combination of field components and is geometry-dependent; it cannot in general be reduced to \(E_R / B\) alone. A correct expression for the \(E\times B\) toroidal angular frequency requires the full poloidal-field geometry.

Typical values. In tokamak core plasmas, \(|E_R|\) is typically in the range \(10^2\)–\(10^4\) V m\(^{-1}\). In the edge and pedestal region, sharp \(E_R\) wells of order \(10^4\)–\(10^5\) V m\(^{-1}\) are observed, associated with the L–H transition and suppression of turbulence.

Sign convention: Positive when the electric field points in the direction of increasing major radius \(R\) (i.e., outward from the machine symmetry axis).

docs.title: toroidal_component_of_electric_field
docs.text:
Projection of the plasma electric field onto the toroidal direction \(\hat{\phi}\), governing the parallel current drive and Ohmic heating in the toroidal circuit.

The toroidal electric field component \(E_\phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\phi}\) is the component of the total electric field aligned with the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\) in the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. It is the primary driver of Ohmic plasma current via \(\mathbf{j} = \sigma \mathbf{E}\), where \(\sigma\) is the parallel plasma conductivity, and enters the toroidal loop voltage equation \(V_{\rm loop} = 2\pi R \, E_\phi\), where \(R\) is the major radius. In the presence of a changing poloidal magnetic flux \(\psi\), Faraday's law gives \(E_\phi = -(2\pi R)^{-1} \partial \psi / \partial t\), directly linking the toroidal field to flux-surface evolution during current ramp-up or ramp-down. Typical magnitudes range from a few tens of mV/m during steady H-mode to several V/m during disruptions or aggressive current ramps. It is inferred from magnetic loop measurements and equilibrium reconstruction, or computed self-consistently in transport codes from the current diffusion equation. The companion components poloidal_component_of_electric_field and radial_component_of_electric_field complete the decomposition of the full field vector.

Sign convention: Positive when \(E_\phi\) points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\).

docs.title: momentum_convection_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
docs.text:
Effective scalar radial convective velocity in the momentum transport equation arising from the diamagnetic drift of a charged species. Represents the net radial advection speed of momentum density across flux surfaces due to pressure-gradient-driven cross-field drifts.

In fluid descriptions of magnetized plasma transport, the momentum flux across flux surfaces contains a convective contribution proportional to a radial convective velocity \(v_\mathrm{dia}\). This quantity is defined as the effective radial projection of the diamagnetic drift that enters the radial momentum transport equation:

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(m_s n_s u_{s,\parallel}) + \frac{1}{V'} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} \left[ V' \left( -D \frac{\partial (m_s n_s u_{s,\parallel})}{\partial \rho} + v_\mathrm{dia} \, m_s n_s u_{s,\parallel} \right) \right] = \ldots\]

where \(\rho\) is a radial flux-surface label (e.g., \(\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}\)), \(V'= \partial V/\partial\rho\) is the flux-surface volume derivative, \(m_s\) is the species mass, \(n_s\) the density, \(u_{s,\parallel}\) the parallel flow velocity, and \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient.

The stored scalar \(v_\mathrm{dia}\) (in m/s) is the effective radial convective speed extracted from the full vector diamagnetic drift. The underlying vector diamagnetic drift velocity for a charged species with charge \(q_s\) is:

\[\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \frac{- abla p_s \times \mathbf{B}}{q_s n_s B^2}\]

where \(p_s\) is the species pressure and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the magnetic field. The scalar \(v_\mathrm{dia}\) stored in the transport IDS is the flux-surface-averaged radial component of this drift projected onto the minor-radius direction \(\hat{\rho}\) (outward from the magnetic axis in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame):

\[v_\mathrm{dia} = \langle \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},s} \cdot \hat{\rho} \rangle\]

where the angle brackets denote the flux-surface average. The precise numerical value depends on geometry and the transport model performing the flux-surface averaging.

Typical magnitudes for ion species in tokamak plasmas are \(10^1\)–\(10^4\) m/s, with larger values in steep-gradient regions such as the edge pedestal.

Note: The linked DD path plasma_transport/model/profiles_1d/neutral/state/momentum/v/diamagnetic stores this quantity for neutral states. In standard physics, neutral particles do not experience the magnetic diamagnetic drift. When a value appears under a neutral species path, it represents an effective convective velocity assigned by the transport model's fluid closure (e.g., from charge-exchange coupling or an effective neutral fluid approximation), not a direct magnetic drift of the neutrals themselves.

The quantity is evaluated at each radial location on the transport grid associated with the plasma transport IDS.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective radial convective velocity is directed outward, away from the magnetic axis along the direction of increasing minor radius.
