docs.title: parallel_component_of_ion_momentum_flow_damping_rate
docs.text:
Rate at which the component of ion fluid momentum flow along the local magnetic field direction is dissipated by collisional friction or neoclassical viscosity in the plasma transport model.

The parallel component of the ion momentum flow damping rate, $ u_{\parallel,\rm damp}$, is the scalar coefficient appearing in the parallel projection of the ion momentum sink term:

\[\left(\frac{\partial (m_i n_i u_{i\parallel})}{\partial t}\right)_{\rm damp} = - u_{\parallel,\rm damp}\, m_i n_i u_{i\parallel}\]

where \(m_i\) is the ion mass, \(n_i\) is the ion number density, and \(u_{i\parallel} = \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \hat{b}\) is the ion fluid velocity projected onto the unit vector \(\hat{b}\) along the magnetic field. The parallel direction is special in magnetized plasmas because parallel momentum transport is governed predominantly by ion–ion collisions and parallel viscosity, whereas perpendicular components are additionally regulated by neoclassical poloidal-flow damping (Stringer spin-up and neoclassical flow damping). Physically, $ u_{\parallel,\rm damp}$ encapsulates contributions from ion–ion collisional friction, parallel viscous damping, and any neoclassical effects projected onto the field-aligned direction. Typical values in the tokamak core range from \(10^2\) to \(10^5\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) depending on collisionality and plasma density; in the high-collisionality (Pfirsch–Schlüter) regime the rate approaches the ion–ion collision frequency $ u_{ii}$. This quantity is a member of the directional decomposition family of ion_momentum_flow_damping_rate, which also includes the radial_component_of_ion_momentum_flow_damping_rate, poloidal_component_of_ion_momentum_flow_damping_rate, and toroidal_component_of_ion_momentum_flow_damping_rate. In transport codes it is computed from neoclassical models (e.g. NCLASS, NEO) or from collisional closure schemes applied along flux surfaces.

Sign convention: Positive when the damping acts to reduce the parallel ion momentum, i.e. when \(u_{i\parallel}\) and the resulting momentum sink have the same sign as \(u_{i\parallel}\) itself (damping coefficient positive definite).

Unit: s^-1

Kind: scalar

docs.title: derivative_of_electron_density_with_respect_to_normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
docs.text:
First radial derivative of the total electron number density (thermal plus non-thermal) with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\), capturing how electron density varies across flux surfaces.

The quantity \(\partial n_e / \partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\) gives the radial gradient of the total electron number density — including both thermal and non-thermal (fast) contributions — with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \in [0, 1]\), where \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 0\) at the magnetic axis and \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 1\) at the last closed flux surface. Because \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\) is dimensionless, the derivative carries the same dimensions as density itself. This gradient appears directly in the electron particle transport equation,

\[\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t} + abla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e = S_e,\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e\) is the electron particle flux and \(S_e\) is the source term; the Fickian diffusive flux is proportional to this gradient via the electron particle diffusion coefficient. In transport solver codes, the derivative is evaluated numerically on the 1-D radial grid in \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\) from density profiles obtained via Thomson scattering, interferometry, or reflectometry. Typical core gradients in H-mode tokamaks range from \(-10^{20}\) to \(-10^{19}\) m\(^{-3}\) per unit \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\), with steeper pedestals approaching \(-10^{21}\) m\(^{-3}\). The second-order analog is second_derivative_of_electron_density_with_respect_to_normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate, and the corresponding ion-species quantity is derivative_of_ion_density_with_respect_to_normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate.

Sign convention: Positive when electron density increases in the direction of increasing \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\), i.e. toward the plasma boundary.

docs.title: tendency_of_fast_electron_density
docs.text:
Rate of change of the suprathermal (non-thermal) electron number density with respect to time, representing the net source minus sink of fast electrons at each flux surface in the transport solver.

The tendency of fast electron density, \(\partial n_{\rm fast,e} / \partial t\), where \(n_{\rm fast,e}\) is the number density of suprathermal electrons (those with energies substantially exceeding the thermal energy \(k_B T_e\)), quantifies how the non-thermal electron population evolves in time. This quantity appears as the left-hand side of the fast electron continuity equation in transport codes, balancing sources such as runaway generation, beam injection, and wave-driven acceleration against sinks including collisional slowing-down (thermalization), radial transport, and orbit losses. It is distinct from tendency_of_electron_density, which covers the total electron population (thermal plus non-thermal), and complements tendency_of_ion_state_fast_particle_density, the analogous quantity for non-thermal ions. Radial profiles are resolved in the normalized toroidal flux coordinate \(\rho_{\rm tor,norm}\); the derivative_of_fast_electron_density_with_respect_to_normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate provides the spatial gradient used alongside this tendency in implicit time-advance schemes. Typical magnitudes during sawtooth-driven fast electron redistribution or NBI injection are of order \(10^{16}\)–\(10^{19}\) m\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\) depending on plasma density and auxiliary heating power.

Sign convention: Positive when the fast electron density is increasing in time (net source exceeds net sink).

Unit: m^-3

Kind: scalar

Status: Draft

docs.title: second_derivative_of_fast_electron_density_with_respect_to_normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
docs.text:
Second derivative of the fast (suprathermal) electron number density with respect to the normalized toroidal flux coordinate \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\), characterizing the radial curvature of the non-thermal electron density profile across nested flux surfaces.

The fast electron population consists of suprathermal electrons whose kinetic energy substantially exceeds the bulk thermal energy, arising from sources such as runaway electron generation, radio-frequency heating, or beam injection. This quantity is the second derivative \(\partial^2 n_{\mathrm{fe}} / \partial \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}^2\), where \(n_{\mathrm{fe}}\) is the fast electron number density and \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} / \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,edge}}}\) is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate (dimensionless, ranging from 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary). Although the coordinate \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\) is dimensionless, differentiating a density quantity twice with respect to it preserves the units of number density. The second derivative quantifies the local concavity of the fast electron density profile and appears as a higher-order term in transport solver discretizations, entering the radial diffusion operator for the fast electron continuity equation alongside the first derivative captured by first derivative of fast electron density. The analogous quantity for the total electron population is second derivative of electron density, and the corresponding fast ion quantity is the second derivative of fast ion density. Typical fast electron densities in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas range from \(10^{16}\) to \(10^{18}\) m\(^{-3}\); the magnitude of the second derivative depends sensitively on source localization and transport properties. This quantity is not directly measured but is computed numerically from the radial fast electron density profile during transport solver iterations.

Sign convention: Positive when the fast electron density profile is concave upward (i.e., the profile curves away from the magnetic axis) with respect to increasing \(\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\).

docs.title: tendency_of_ion_state_density
docs.text:
Time derivative of total ion number density (thermal plus non-thermal) for a specific ionic charge state, representing the local rate of change of charge-state population in the transport solver continuity equation.

The tendency of ion charge-state density quantifies \(\partial n_{z,s} / \partial t\), where \(n_{z,s}\) is the total (thermal plus non-thermal) number density of ions of species \(z\) in charge state \(s\). This quantity appears as the time-advance term in the per-charge-state ion continuity equation solved by transport codes, capturing sources and sinks from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and cross-field transport simultaneously. It differs from tendency of ion density, which sums over all charge states to give the species-integrated continuity source, and from tendency of ion state fast particle density, which isolates only the non-thermal (fast) component for the same charge state. Typical magnitudes in core tokamak transport simulations range from \(10^{16}\) to \(10^{20}\) m\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\) depending on plasma density, heating power, and the charge state considered, with higher charge states of impurity ions exhibiting sharper transients during pellet injection or disruption precursors. The second radial derivative of the same density profile is documented under second derivative of ion state density with respect to normalized toroidal flux coordinate, which enters the diffusive term of the same continuity equation. Analogous electron-side quantities include tendency of electron density and tendency of fast electron density.

docs.title: co_passing_particle_density
docs.text:
Total particle number density (thermal plus non-thermal) of the co-passing population, comprising particles whose guiding-center orbits circulate toroidally in the same direction as the net plasma current. Distinct from the trapped and counter-passing populations that together make up the total particle density.

The co-passing particle density \(n_\mathrm{co}\) is the number density of particles whose guiding-center motion executes complete toroidal transits in the co-current direction, i.e., in the direction of increasing toroidal angle \(\phi\) when the plasma current \(I_p\) is positive (flowing in the \(+\hat{\phi}\) direction of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame). Classification as co-passing versus counter-passing depends on the sign of the parallel velocity projected onto the local magnetic field direction weighted by the direction of the net toroidal current, and not merely on the sign of the local \(v_\parallel\): a particle is co-passing if its orbit-averaged toroidal angular velocity shares the sign of \(I_p\).

The density is computed as the zeroth moment of the co-passing part of the distribution function \(f_\mathrm{co}(\mathbf{r}, v_\parallel, v_\perp)\) over velocity space:

\[n_\mathrm{co}(R,Z) = \int_{v_\parallel / v > v_{\parallel,\mathrm{trap}}(R,Z)} f_\mathrm{co}\, 2\pi v_\perp\, dv_\perp\, dv_\parallel\]

where the lower limit on \(v_\parallel\) is set by the trapping condition at the local flux surface. Both thermal and non-thermal (suprathermal, beam-injected, and fast) particles contribute.

Typical values in a tokamak core range from \(10^{17}\) to \(10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) depending on species, plasma current, and heating scenario. In nearly axisymmetric plasmas with a symmetric distribution function the co- and counter-passing densities are nearly equal; asymmetric heating (e.g., co-directed neutral beam injection) or current drive creates a net imbalance.

This quantity is stored in the IMAS distributions IDS at the path distributions/distribution/profiles_2d/co_passing/density (unit: m\(^{-3}\)), where the co_passing node distinguishes this population from the counter_passing and trapped sub-populations. The total particle density is the sum of co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped densities integrated over the full distribution.

docs.title: counter_passing_particle_density
docs.text:
Total particle number density of the counter-passing population (thermal plus non-thermal), comprising particles whose guiding-center parallel velocity is directed opposite to the plasma current along the magnetic field. The orbit-class boundary is defined by the local pitch angle at the trapping-passing boundary, typically |v_parallel/v| > lambda_crit, and is model-dependent.

The counter-passing particle density \(n_{\mathrm{ctr}}\) is the number density of all particles (thermal and non-thermal combined) whose guiding-center parallel velocity \(v_\|\) is directed antiparallel to the net plasma current \(I_p\) along the magnetic-field line.

More precisely, the passing–trapping boundary is set at the critical pitch-angle cosine \(\lambda_c = v_{\|}/v\) for which the particle orbit just closes without mirroring; particles with \(|\lambda| > \lambda_c\) are passing, and among those the counter-passing subset satisfies \(\mathrm{sgn}(v_\|) = -\mathrm{sgn}(B_\phi \cdot I_p / |B_\phi \cdot I_p|)\), i.e. their parallel velocity opposes the field-aligned component of the current. The precise value of \(\lambda_c\) depends on the magnetic geometry and the distribution-function model used; it is not a universal constant.

The total particle density partitions as

\[n = n_{\mathrm{co}} + n_{\mathrm{ctr}} + n_{\mathrm{trapped}},\]

where \(n_{\mathrm{co}}\) is the co-passing density, \(n_{\mathrm{ctr}}\) is this quantity, and \(n_{\mathrm{trapped}}\) is the trapped-particle density. This bookkeeping identity holds by construction for any distribution-function discretization that assigns each marker to exactly one orbit class.

Typical values range from \(10^{17}\) m\(^{-3}\) (low-density auxiliary-heated plasmas) to \(\sim 10^{20}\) m\(^{-3}\) (high-density core). Counter-passing fractions relative to \(n\) depend on collisionality regime and heating geometry; in a banana-regime tokamak at moderate aspect ratio the trapped fraction is \(\sim \epsilon^{1/2}\) (\(\epsilon = r/R\) local inverse aspect ratio), so \(n_{\mathrm{ctr}} \approx n_{\mathrm{co}} \approx (1 - \epsilon^{1/2}) n / 2\) under isotropic conditions.

docs.title: fast_ion_pressure
docs.text:
Anisotropic kinetic pressure of the fast (non-thermal) ion population, capturing the full pressure tensor arising from non-Maxwellian velocity distributions of energetic ions in a magnetized plasma.

Fast ions — alpha particles, neutral-beam-injected ions, and ICRH-accelerated ions — develop strongly anisotropic velocity distributions that cannot be characterized by a single scalar pressure. The fast-ion pressure tensor is most naturally decomposed along and perpendicular to the local magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\), yielding two independent scalar components: the parallel pressure \(p_{\parallel,f} = m_f \int v_{\parallel}^2 f_f \, d^3v\) and the perpendicular pressure \(p_{\perp,f} = \frac{m_f}{2} \int v_{\perp}^2 f_f \, d^3v\), where \(m_f\) is the fast-ion mass and \(f_f\) is the fast-ion distribution function. The isotropic (trace) contribution to the total pressure balance is \(p_f = (p_{\parallel,f} + 2\,p_{\perp,f})/3\). In ITER-class deuterium–tritium plasmas, fast-ion pressures can reach \(10^4\)–\(10^5\) Pa in the core, representing a significant fraction of the total MHD pressure and thus affecting equilibrium reconstruction and stability analysis. The distribution function is computed from Fokker–Planck or Monte Carlo codes (e.g., using distributions of particle populations), and validated against fast-ion diagnostics such as neutral-particle analyzers and collective Thomson scattering. The directional components are accessed individually as parallel_component_of_fast_ion_pressure and perpendicular_component_of_fast_ion_pressure; the analogous quantity for fast neutrals arising from charge-exchange reactions is fast_neutral_pressure.

Sign convention: Positive when the fast-ion kinetic energy density is positive, which is always the case for a physical distribution function.

docs.title: vertical_component_of_electron_velocity
docs.text:
Projection of the bulk electron fluid velocity onto the vertical \(Z\)-axis of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, representing the net upward or downward motion of the electron population at each point in the plasma.

The vertical component \(v_{e,Z} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{Z}\) isolates the \(Z\)-directed part of the electron bulk fluid velocity, where \(\mathbf{v}_e\) is the electron fluid velocity and \(\hat{Z}\) is the unit vector along the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame. This quantity appears in the electron fluid momentum equation and contributes to cross-field transport in regions with strong vertical gradients, such as the divertor and scrape-off layer. In tokamak edge and divertor plasmas, \(v_{e,Z}\) can reach \(10^3\)–\(10^5\) m/s, depending on the parallel flow projected along field lines with significant vertical inclination. It is computed from fluid or kinetic transport simulations and can be inferred indirectly from spectroscopic Doppler measurements combined with magnetic geometry. The corresponding ion and neutral counterparts are given by vertical_component_of_ion_velocity and vertical_component_of_neutral_velocity; the mass-weighted mixture velocity is vertical_component_of_center_of_mass_velocity. The parent quantity electron_velocity provides the full vector from which this component is projected.

Sign convention: Positive when the electron fluid velocity is directed in the \(+Z\) direction (upward, away from the divertor toward the top of the machine).

docs.title: vertical_component_of_ion_velocity
docs.text:
Projection of the bulk ion fluid velocity onto the vertical \(Z\)-axis of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, representing the net upward or downward motion of the ion population at each point in the plasma.

The vertical velocity component \(v_{Z,i} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{Z}\) measures the ion fluid motion along the \(Z\)-axis (height direction) of the right-handed cylindrical \((R, \phi, Z)\) frame, where \(R\) is major radius and \(Z\) is vertical height. It is one component of the full ion_velocity vector and is required in multi-fluid transport models to capture poloidal and cross-field ion dynamics on unstructured plasma-boundary grids. In the edge and scrape-off layer, \(v_{Z,i}\) enters the ion continuity equation \(\partial n_i/\partial t + abla \cdot (n_i \mathbf{v}_i) = S_i\), where \(n_i\) (m\(^{-3}\)) is ion density and \(S_i\) is the particle source, and contributes to the divergence of the ion particle flux. Typical magnitudes range from tens to hundreds of m s\(^{-1}\) in the edge plasma and can reach \(\sim 10^4\) m s\(^{-1}\) near the divertor targets. It is computed in fluid transport codes and can be compared against the analogous vertical_component_of_electron_velocity and vertical_component_of_neutral_velocity to characterize inter-species flow differences. The vertical_component_of_center_of_mass_velocity provides the mass-weighted average over all species for comparison with the ion-specific component.

Sign convention: Positive when the ion fluid velocity is directed in the \(+Z\) direction (upward, away from the machine midplane).
